# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 67 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 67 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_067_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 6, Part 5 — Why Good People Suffer

**67:1** "Lord," I asked, "why do some of God's servants live righteously and don't sin, yet they still experience so many torments and hardships in their lives?" "How long are you going to be slow to understand things?" he said. "You ask about everything — you never stop asking. You're too persistent."

**67:2** "Now listen," he said. "Don't think for a moment that people who seem to always do good and avoid sin are actually sinless. They sin every single day — but the sins are small ones: in what they say, in what they do, even in what they think. And because their sins are small, the Lord doesn't punish them heavily. He gives them only light afflictions."

**67:3** "But those who have committed great sins, piled one on another, receive much heavier torments — they're handed over to the angel of punishment for a long stretch of time." "But lord," I said, "will even those people — the ones who sinned greatly and are being punished — will they eventually be saved?" "Yes," he said, "but it's going to take a long time."

**67:4** "Lord," I said, "I'd like to understand the different types of torments and adversities. Are they really different from each other?" "Yes, they are," he said, "and I'll show you which ones apply to which kinds of people."

**67:5** "The torments and adversities that come on people in this life include losses of all kinds, aimless wandering, various illnesses, every kind of disturbance and turmoil, painful separation from friends and loved ones, poverty, and all manner of trouble. These are the afflictions that God's servants must go through in their lives. The Lord, who is abundantly merciful, uses these to discipline them so they can be purified."

---

*PNEUMA renders for contemporary clarity and accessibility, capturing the theodicy of suffering as corrective discipline in Similitude 6.*
